blocks.title: Key Takeaways
items: Horticulture serves as the economic backbone of the Kashmir region.
Handicrafts constitute a core element of Jammu & Kashmir's industrial and cultural identity.
Tourism in J&K relies heavily on major leisure destinations and significant religious tourism circuits.
The Indus Waters Treaty (1960) remains a crucial framework for regional water resource distribution and infrastructure.

cells: Agriculture, Horticulture, Animal Husbandry, Forestry — ~18-20% of GSDP
J&K highly dependent on central funds (Special Category Status previously)

items: J&K is predominantly rural with ~65% population engaged in agriculture/horticulture
Major Kharif crops: Paddy (dominant), Maize, Bajra
Major Rabi crops: Wheat, Barley, Mustard
Paddy: Kashmir Valley; Jammu plains (major paddy areas)
Wheat: Grown in Jammu; winter crop
Apple: J&K (mainly Kashmir) accounts for ~75-80% of India's apple production; Sopore is Asia's 2nd largest apple market
Saffron: Pampore (near Anantnag/Pulwama); GI tag obtained; 'Kashmiri Kesar' is world's finest saffron; India's only saffron-growing area; NaBH (National Saffron Mission)
Walnut: J&K is India's largest walnut producer; Kashmir walnuts famous worldwide
Cherry: Sopore, Shopian area; 3 varieties — local, hybrid, yellow
Pear: Kulgam, Shopian
Almond: Budgam, Anantnag
Strawberry: Being promoted in Kashmir
Lavender cultivation: CSIR-IIIM Jammu leading 'Aroma Mission'; replacing traditional crops with lavender, passionfruit, etc. in Jammu hills
Cattle rearing; Crossbred Jersey and Holstein cows
Buffalo: Murrah buffalo farming promoted
Sheep: Bakarwal & Gujjar communities rear sheep; 'Pashmina' from Changthangi goats in Ladakh
Pashmina: World-famous fine wool; GI tag; from Changthangi goats at 4,500 m altitude; only hand-spun and woven
Yak: Ladakh; used for transport, milk, and wool
Fish: Trout fishing in Kashmir rivers; Mahseer in Jhelum; Fish farming in Dal Lake
Sericulture (Silk): Kashmir known for silk weaving; Mulberry silkworm cultivation

cells: Pashmina/Shahtoosh shawls; Kani shawl (woven with wooden bobbins); GI tagged
Hand-knotted; intricate Persian designs; major export item
Srinagar; painted lacquerware; boxes, vases, decorative items
Furniture, decorative items; unique to Kashmir; GI tagged
Thangka paintings, silver jewelry, wood carvings, masks

items: Hydro Power: J&K has massive hydro potential (~20,000 MW); major projects: Baglihar (900 MW on Chenab), Uri-I (480 MW), Uri-II (240 MW), Dulhasti (390 MW), Salal (690 MW), Kishanganga (330 MW)
Cement: Khrew (Kashmir); Wanpoh; limestone deposits in Udhampur
Resin & Turpentine: Forest-based industry
Food Processing: Apple-based; juice, cider, dried fruits
Pharmaceuticals: Growing sector in Jammu
IT/Software: J&K IT Policy; IT parks in Srinagar & Jammu; 'Digital J&K' mission
Tourism Industry: Major economic driver — see Section 4.5

blocks.content: Tourism is the backbone of Kashmir's economy. J&K attracts millions of tourists annually.

items: Gulmarg: 'Meadow of Flowers'; skiing capital of India; Gondola (Phase I – 2,600 m; Phase II – 4,200 m); Golf course (world's highest 18-hole)
Pahalgam: 'Valley of Shepherds'; Liddar river; Amarnath Yatra base; Baisaran, Betaab Valley
Sonamarg: 'Meadow of Gold'; gateway to Ladakh; Thajiwas Glacier
Dal Lake: Houseboats, Shikara rides; Floating vegetable gardens (Rad)
Amarnath Cave Temple: Anantnag; ~3,880 m; Shiva Linga made of ice; Shravan month pilgrimage; SASB (Shri Amarnathji Shrine Board) manages
Vaishno Devi: Reasi district; ~7 million pilgrims annually; SVBTT (Shri Mata Vaishno Devi Shrine Board) manages; one of India's most visited pilgrimages
Leh-Ladakh: Adventure tourism — trekking, rafting, motorcycle trips; Pangong Lake, Nubra Valley, Zanskar Valley
Patnitop: Hill resort; Udhampur; snow in winter; paragliding
Doodhpathri: 'Valley of Milk'; Budgam; pristine meadows
Yusmarg: 'Jesus Meadow'; Budgam; peaceful meadow; horse rides
Amarnath: Shaiva pilgrimage; holy cave; naturally occurring ice Shiva Linga
Vaishno Devi: Goddess temple in Trikuta Hills; Katra base camp
Kheer Bhawani: Ganderbal; goddess temple; spring festival
Shankaracharya Temple: Srinagar; hilltop Shiva temple; 1,100 ft above valley
Martand Sun Temple ruins: Mattan, Anantnag
Hazratbal Shrine: Srinagar; Moi-e-Muqaddas (Holy Relic of Prophet)
Charar-e-Sharief: Budgam; shrine of Sheikh Noor-ud-Din Wali (Nund Rishi)
Hemis Monastery: Leh; largest & wealthiest monastery; annual Hemis Festival
Indus Waters Treaty (1960) provisions, rivers involved, and signed dates.
Economic contribution of horticulture and traditional handicrafts in J&K.
Key tourist destinations, religious tourism circuits, and major infrastructure developments in the region.
Signed between India & Pakistan on September 19, 1960; brokered by World Bank
India: Rights over 3 eastern rivers — Ravi, Beas, Sutlej (total ~33 MAF)
Pakistan: Rights over 3 western rivers — Indus, Jhelum, Chenab (~80 MAF)
India can use western rivers for run-of-river hydro projects with storage limits
PERMANENT INDUS COMMISSION: Annual meetings; dispute resolution mechanism
India's major projects on western rivers: Baglihar, Salal, Kishanganga, Ratle (under construction)
Pakistan raised disputes at Permanent Court of Arbitration (PCA) over Kishanganga & Ratle projects
India suspended IWT after Pahalgam Terror Attack (April 2025) citing changed circumstances
